new_statements.quote: En tzotzil existen dos tipos de acentuación prosódica: A. Las palabras se acentúan sobre la primera sílaba de la raíz, sea ésta simple o compuesta. En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento. Ejemplos: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc ustedes tienen misericordia de nosotros / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué los hombres [...] B. La última sílaba de una oración se acentúa con un aumento en el tono de la última sílaba y un desvanecimiento del mismo. [...] Por el hecho de que la acentuación obedece estas reglas, no es necesario indicarla en forma escrita en el idioma.
new_statements.translation: In Tzotzil there are two kinds of prosodic accentuation: A. Words are accented on the first syllable of the root, whether simple or compound. In strings of several syllables one further syllable is accented, so that never more than three syllables in a row appear without accent. Examples: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc 'you (pl.) have mercy on us' / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué 'the men' [...] B. The last syllable of a sentence is accented with a rise in the pitch of that last syllable and a fading of it. [...] Because accentuation obeys these rules, it is not necessary to mark it in writing in the language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the lexical root, so prefixes (aspect/person markers, articles) are skipped; in long polysyllabic strings an extra stress is added so that no more than three unstressed syllables run together (in the examples the root-initial syllable is marked with a diaeresis, c'ü / vï, and the added stresses with acute accents, nún, tíc / qué). Separately, the final syllable of a sentence carries a pitch rise-and-fall; the final syllable of a preceding subordinate clause or noun phrase gets the rise without the fall. Laughlin 1975:23 (Zinacantán, same 'central' dialect area as Chenalhó by his classification) and Haviland 1981:14 (Zinacantán) state the same two-level system: root-initial word stress plus phrase-final prominence, with isolated words heard as final-stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento' — an additional stress is inserted so that at most three unstressed syllables occur in sequence (examples cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc; li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué). Laughlin and Haviland mention no secondary word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for the word rule. Laughlin 1975:23 (Zinacantán) notes that in isolation forms stress is not final in affective verbs with -luh, first-person-plural-exclusive suffixed forms and reduplicated disyllabic stems. Haviland 1981:14: particles are unaccented unless phrase-final.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root-initial) versus sentence/phrase level (final syllable, pitch rise); examples are orthographic and accents were added only to guide the reader; the book states stress is not written. The statement is made for 'tzotzil' as a language, in a San Andrés-based dictionary that samples Chenalhó variants; it is not a Chenalhó-specific description.
new_statements.identity_note: tzot1263 is the Glottolog bookkeeping entry for retired ISO 639-3 code tze 'Chenalhó Tzotzil' (Tzotzil Ch'enalo'), merged into tzo = tzot1259 by ISO change request 2008-061; Glottolog 5.1 attaches no descriptive references to it. No Chenalhó-specific stress statement was found. The quoted statement comes from the ILV dictionary of the San Andrés Larráinzar dialect (= tzot1260), which explicitly samples Chenalhó ('Ch'en') as one of four additional variants and whose grammar was proofread by Manuel Arias Pérez of Chenalhó; the accent rule is stated for Tzotzil as a whole. Laughlin 1975 (Zinacantán = tzot1264) places Chenalhó in the same central dialect area as Zinacantán and gives the same root-initial + phrase-final system. Glottolog's only Chenalhó-coded description is Hopkins 1967 on the neighbouring Chalchihuitán variety (not obtained).

sources.citation: Haviland, John B. 1981. Sk'op Sotz'leb: El Tzotzil de San Lorenzo Zinacantán. México: UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Filológicas, Centro de Estudios Mayas. Cap. I 'Notas sobre la fonología', p. 14.
sources.note: p. 14: 'El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz; además hay un acento aun más fuerte que acompaña la última sílaba de una frase o una oración (puede consistir en una sola palabra, pronunciada aisladamente...)'. Zinacantán only; no Chenalhó remark.

sources.note: p. 23: 'Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables... In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase.' Zinacantán dialect; the introduction (scanned lines 908-916) maps Tzotzil into five dialect areas and puts Chenalhó in the same central area as Zinacantán, Chamula and Mitontic.
